provenance: Acquired directly from the artist. | Private American collection. | Property of a Gentleman. | | The present composition, painted circa 1917, revisits an earlier work completed during Wilhelm Kuhnert's second expedition to Africa in 1905. While both compositions share similarities, Two lions at watch is notably larger and places greater emphasis on the two lions, positioning them as the central figures within the vast African environment. Kuhnert embarked on his first journey to Africa in 1891, he was then commissioned to visit the German and English colonial territories of East and South Africa on safari in 1905 and 1911-12 after gaining popularity. His portrayals of African wildlife, inspired by renowned German animal painter Richard Friese, depict wild animals in their natural settings. Lions held a special significance for Kuhnert, earning him the nickname "Lion-Kuhnert" for his exceptional affinity with the species. | | The authenticity of this work has been previously confirmed by Dr Angelika Grettmann-Werner and is registered in the catalogue raisonné no. 4028.

provenance: Acquired directly from the artist, thence by decent. | Private collection, UK. | | A passionate huntsman with an exceptional eye for the sporting world, John Emms had the rare gift of breathing life into his subjects. Nowhere was his talent more evident than in his depictions of dogs. He captured not only the weight and form of each animal but also its unique personality. Emms was known to visit the kennels daily, returning to his studio with one hound after another to make preliminary sketches that would later form the foundation of his larger compositions. | | Born in Blofield, Norfolk, the son of artist Henry William Emms, John moved to London as a young man, where he served as studio assistant to Frederic, Lord Leighton. In the early 1860s, while assisting Leighton on the fresco The Wise and Foolish Virgins at St. Michael and All Angels Church in Lyndhurst, Emms is thought to have painted the owl beneath the outstretched arms of the angel to the right of centre. This first encounter with Hampshire proved decisive, setting the course for the rest of his artistic life. By 1872, Emms had begun dividing his time between London and Lyndhurst, and around 1881 he settled in the latter permanently. The natural beauty of the New Forest and the abundance of hunting pursuits offered him endless inspiration. | | A skilled horseman, enthusiastic huntsman and genial companion, he soon became sought after by members of the peerage and landed gentry across Britain for his portraits of horses, hounds and sporting dogs. Emms was as colourful in character as in talent, often seen in his trademark long black cloak and wide-brimmed hat. He and his family led a somewhat bohemian existence; when a painting sold, he would take his wife Fanny and their four children off to London to stay in fine hotels and enjoy the good life. Widely admired in his day, Emms left behind a remarkable and enduring body of work.
